subject: Culture
title: Textile as Wealth
description: A micro-lesson that makes Textile as Wealth usable.

hook.text: In medieval Europe, fabric was so valuable that clothing was listed in wills alongside land and livestock.

buildup.text: Before mass production, a single garment could take months to weave, dye, and sew by hand.

discovery.text: The Silk Road existed because Chinese silk was worth its weight in gold to Roman aristocrats.

twist.text: Sumptuary laws banned commoners from wearing fabrics reserved for nobles. Velvet was literally illegal for peasants.

climax.text: The Industrial Revolution made cloth cheap. For the first time, everyone could afford to look aspirational.

punchline.text: Clothing was the original status symbol—before cars, before houses.

quiz.question: What were laws restricting clothing by social class called?

details.summary: For most of human history, textiles were a primary form of wealth. Silk was worth more than gold by weight. Purple dye required thousands of sea snails per gram. Clothing was inherited, taxed, and traded as currency across empires.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing textiles as historic wealth reveals why clothing laws, trade wars, and colonial exploitation so often centered on fabric. The fast-fashion era's disposability is historically extraordinary.
takeaways: Textiles served as currency and wealth stores for millennia
Tyrian purple dye cost more per gram than gold
Clothing was commonly inherited and listed in wills

faq.question: Why was silk so valuable in the ancient world?
faq.answer: China guarded silk production secrets for thousands of years, making it rare outside Asia. Silk was lightweight, lustrous, and virtually impossible to replicate. It traveled the Silk Road at enormous markup, sometimes equaling the price of gold by weight.

faq.question: How did textiles function as money?
faq.answer: In many societies, standardized lengths of cloth served as currency. Aztecs used cotton cloaks as a unit of exchange. Viking traders valued fabric alongside silver. Medieval European wills routinely listed individual garments as significant bequests.
